modules.title: Screening & Crushing
checkpoint: I can sketch a partition curve and explain d₅₀, sharpness and imperfection
I know when a distribution-curve model (CYCB) is enough and when the Karra model is needed
I can explain why small particles are harder to break, and what the breakage function describes

modules.title: Separation by Density
checkpoint: I can construct a partition curve from washability data and compute EPM and Ic
I know when to give the model a cut density (Gottfried-Jacobsen) and when a medium density (King & Jukes)
I can explain the cut-point shift and why it grows for fine particles and centrifugal separators
I can explain the stratification constant α and why later stages in series get a higher value
I know the water-balance blind spot of the stratification models — and plan dilution accordingly

modules.title: Separation by Surface Properties
checkpoint: I can fit R∞ and K to bank survey data — and I know why the constants differ between models

I can recognize carrying-capacity-limited flotation from cumulative recovery curves (linear start)
I know FLTK's physical levers: aeration, bubble size, bubble residence time, FTC, dp,max
I can explain why concentrate grades of different minerals are coupled

modules.title: Magnetic Separation & Dewatering

I know the two-component limitation of the LIMS models and where the magnetic phase must sit in the materials definition
I can evaluate a batch settling test: initial slope → velocity → Stokes floc size → thickener capacity
I know why THIC gives no report and what KYNC adds — and the limits of both
I can manage a circuit's water balance with FILT's cake moisture and the thickener overflows

modules.title: Start here: how the course works
The geometallurgical approach
checkpoint: ILO 5 — I can describe the chain from discovery to closure, name who hands what to whom, and point at the hand-over where 10 000 assays meet 5–10 metallurgical samples.
ILO 5 — I can list what a traditional block model carries and what a geometallurgical block model adds, and say what each addition is there to predict.
ILO 1 — I can explain what "every ore body is unique and heterogeneous" means in practice, and name at least four properties in which a deposit varies.
ILO 2 — I can trace a metallurgical response back to its cause through geology, mining, comminution and beneficiation, and say which of those causes are texture-driven.
ILO 5 — I can define geometallurgical domain , explain why domaining is a first-order decision, and give a reason why a grade domain may be the wrong domain for a comminution variable.
ILO 4 — I can distinguish a primary response from a proxy, give an example of each, and explain what has to happen before a proxy may be used in a model.
ILO 4 — I can name the four levels of measurement in a test programme and place a Bond work index, a chemical assay and a plant throughput figure at the right level.

ILO 5 — I can state three decisions a geometallurgical model supports that a grade-only model cannot, and explain in one sentence why "the resource model is not the truth" matters for the project report.

modules.title: Sampling and sampling theory
checkpoint: ILO 5 — I can state the golden rule of correct sampling, and use it to say why a scoop off the top of a stockpile is not a sample.
ILO 5 — I can draw the error chain from primary sampling to assay and say where the largest error normally sits, and why students expect the wrong answer.
ILO 5 — I can distinguish bias from imprecision, and explain why a precise biased result is the more dangerous of the two.
ILO 4 — I can compare drill core, reverse circulation chips, trench and pit samples on size, cost, control and representativeness, and choose between them for a stated purpose.
ILO 2 — I can define the support of a measurement and give two samples that are both unbiased and still not comparable.
ILO 2 — I can read Gy's equation and say, without calculating, which of two ores is harder to sample and why — naming the terms that make the difference.
ILO 5 — I can design a staged crush-and-split scheme for a given lot mass, target error and set of crushers, and defend the mass I keep at each top size.
ILO 5 — I can explain what duplicates and blanks each detect, at roughly what frequency they are inserted, and what redundancy in a survey is for.
ILO 4 — I can say what confidence in a drill-hole dataset actually rests on, and explain why a domain that looks uniform may only be under-sampled.

modules.title: Characterisation methods and tools
checkpoint: ILO 2 — I can list the seven characterisation questions and name at least one method for each, and I can explain why "which minerals" and "how much of each" are different questions.
ILO 2 — I can distinguish qualitative from quantitative mineralogy, and give an example of an identification being wrongly used as a quantification.
ILO 4 — Given any two methods from the comparison table, I can state what each answers, what each is blind to, what sample it needs and roughly how long it takes.
ILO 4 — I can explain why an electron beam and a µ-XRF map both fail to separate magnetite from hematite, and name two methods that succeed.
ILO 1 — I can explain what texture means in a process context, and say which methods see it and which destroy it.
ILO 2 — I can write down the relation between element grades and mineral grades, and use it to convert a copper assay into a chalcopyrite grade.

ILO 5 — I can give three reasons why a quantitative dataset and a qualitative one may legitimately disagree — support, measurand, detection limit, stereology, a shared element across hosts — and say what I would do about it.
ILO 5 — I can plan a small characterisation programme backwards from a decision, and justify why the expensive method appears on ten samples rather than on all of them.

modules.title: Element-to-mineral conversion
checkpoint: I can explain in one paragraph why a geometallurgical model needs mineral abundances rather than element grades, and why we nevertheless start from assays. (ILO2, ILO5)
I can write the element-to-mineral mass balance in both forms, aᵢ = Σⱼ cᵢⱼ mⱼ and a = Cm, and say exactly what one row and one column of C mean. (ILO2)
Given a mineral list and an assay suite, I can say before calculating whether the system is over-determined, square or under-determined, and what that implies for the answer. (ILO2, ILO5)
I can compute a small modal composition by hand by taking the elements in the right order, and explain why the least-squares answer differs from it. (ILO2)
I can back-calculate assays from a modal composition, form the residual, and say what a large residual on one element points to. (ILO2, ILO5)
I can explain why the chemical composition of the minerals is half the answer, and when a stoichiometric end member is not good enough. (ILO2)

I can name the four classic failure modes — a missing mineral, wrong stoichiometry, an element in more than one host, too many minerals for the assays — and for each one say what measurement would resolve it. (ILO2, ILO5)
I can take a calculated modal composition and turn it into a process statement: a maximum recovery, or the impurity grade of a theoretical concentrate. (ILO4)

modules.title: Particle behaviour and liberation
checkpoint: I can explain why a separator acts on particles rather than on minerals, and give an example where two ores with the same modal composition behave differently. (ILO2, ILO3)
For any unit operation in a concentrator I can say whether it is selective for particle size, form, composition or density, and what its products are. (ILO3)
I can define liberated and locked, explain why a liberation threshold is needed, and describe a locked particle by the number and identity of the minerals in it. (ILO2)
Given counts by grade class, I can calculate the amount of mineral, the yield, the cumulative yield, the sample grade and the degree of liberation. (ILO2)

I can read a liberation curve as a ceiling on recovery — including reading off the best recovery available at a given particle composition — and I can compare two curves and say which sample is better liberated. (ILO2, ILO4)
I can distinguish random from preferential breakage, name what makes breakage preferential, and state the four conditions that raise the degree of liberation at a chosen particle size. (ILO2, ILO3)
I can explain why grinding finer is not simply an answer, using the liberation gain on one side and energy, fines and separation efficiency on the other. (ILO4)

I can name the methods used to measure liberation, say what each delivers and what it costs in time and precision, and list three things that must be stated before a liberation number can be believed. (ILO2, ILO5)

modules.title: Geometallurgical test methods
checkpoint: I can distinguish a measurement from a test, and give an example of each from this course. (ILO5)
I can describe the four levels of measurement in a test programme and place any given test at the right level. (ILO5)
I can explain what a primary response is, what a proxy is, and name four properties a proxy must have before it can be used in a block model. (ILO4, ILO5)
I can give two ways a proxy fails — a domain it was never calibrated in, and a correlation that is an artefact of the test work — and say what would have exposed each. (ILO4, ILO5)

I can judge whether a proposed test earns its place, using sample mass, time and cost, precision and repeatability, its correlation with the established method, and where its result enters the model. (ILO4, ILO5)
I can explain why the standard Bond test cannot serve as a variability test, and what specifically the GCT changed in order to serve as one. (ILO3, ILO5)

I can run the GCT evaluation on my own data: 80 % passing sizes from the RRSB diagram, energy corrected for drive efficiency, the linear plot of specific energy against 1/sqrt{x_{80,P}}, and a work index from Bond's law and from the slope. (ILO3)
I can state how well the GCT estimate agrees with a full Bond test, where the agreement is worse, and why sample selection outranks test accuracy in the whole chain. (ILO2, ILO5)

modules.title: Modelling, simulation and process metallurgy
checkpoint: I can name the three ingredients of a flowsheet model — streams, units and a material definition — and explain what a modelling level is and what it costs to raise one. (ILO5)
I can distinguish a transformation unit from a separation unit and give the parameters each needs. (ILO3)
For any unit parameter I am given, I can say whether it is a setting, a machine calibration or an ore property — and therefore whether it may change when the ore changes. (ILO5)
I can use Bond's equation to convert a work index and a size reduction into a specific energy, and then into a throughput at fixed installed power. (ILO3)
I can close a two-product mass balance from three assays, compute mass pull and recovery, and say when the formula becomes unreliable. (ILO3)
I can state three things a steady-state simulation predicts well and three it cannot predict at all. (ILO5)
I can explain what a concentrate customer pays for, name penalty elements and say where they end up in a smelter — gas, slag or metal. (ILO4)
Given a concentrate specification and an ore's mineralogy, I can argue which process route is defensible and why. (ILO2, ILO4)

modules.title: Economic appraisal
checkpoint: I can follow one tonne of rock along the value chain and name where material and value are lost at each step. (ILO5)
I can build a net smelter return from a concentrate tonnage and grade, and explain each of the four deductions and what it is charged on. (ILO4)
I can say what a penalty element costs a producer, and connect it back to why the smelter cares. (ILO4)
I can define both cut-off grades, say which is lower and explain why the mining cost is absent from one of them. (ILO4)
I can compute a net present value from a stream of cash flows and explain why a tonne mined in year two is worth more than the same tonne in year twelve. (ILO5)
I can show, with numbers, how a change in metallurgical recovery moves both the NPV and the cut-off grade. (ILO2, ILO5)
I can explain why throughput enters the economics through Bond's equation, and what a harder ore domain does to a fixed-power plant's annual cash flow. (ILO3)
Given several ore domains with different recoveries and hardnesses, I can rank them by value and defend which of them are ore at all. (ILO2, ILO4)
